column3: Directly repeats regret over what was neglected when the Hour arrives.
Uses the same neglect language within acknowledged prior failure and responsibility.
Frames each self's conduct before the common return and disclosure to God.
Immediate sequel gives the next belated excuse: wished-for guidance after the threshold.
Opens the same passage by answering self-inflicted excess with a call not to despair.
Shares neglect language, but concerns false claims and being left for the Fire.
False speech about God does not clarify regret, neglect, or mockery in the focus.
Guidance toward good action only indirectly contrasts the focus's belated wish to be among the doers of good.
Directly depicts mockery and its reversal upon those who mock believing givers.
The self's knowledge of what it sent ahead and left behind supports final personal reckoning.
Immediate prior command to return and submit before unhelped punishment defines the missed opportunity.
Its instruction for upright speech in inheritance protection is unrelated to the focus's final regret.
The earlier state of heedlessness only broadly resembles neglect before guidance.
Immediate sequel supplies the third belated counterfactual: a return to become a doer of good.
The self-reproaching soul closely supports culpable self-recognition, though not the final scene.
Its spatial reference to Moses' western side is not the focus's neglect in relation to God.
Acting with what is better lightly contrasts the focus's delayed desire to be among the doers of good.
Moses' declaration of messengerhood does not illuminate the focus's regret or mockery.
Every self knowing what it brought forward closely parallels final self-disclosure.
Immediate prior command to follow the best revelation before sudden punishment explains the neglected response.
Shows mocking of Noah before the outcome reverses the mockers' judgment.
Identifies the revelation as an irreversible regret for disbelievers.
The forced reconstitution scene completes the irreversible threshold named in the passage.
Its nearness to God and unwearied worship contrast only loosely with neglect of God's claim.
Explicitly grounds final recompense in what each self earned.
A historical restoration is only a distant analogue to the wished-for second turn.
Being kept away from the Fire has only indirect relevance to the focus's failed repentance.
The imposed earthly exclusion and appointment do not clarify the focus's final confession.
Immediate divine reply identifies denied signs, arrogance, and disbelief as the basis of the excuse.
Neglect of remembrance and an excessive course provide a concrete present form of the focus's failure.
Jesus' truthful testimony and divine knowledge do not develop the focus's regret or mockery.
The passage's contrast between voluntary return and God's taking of souls supports the irreversible threshold.
Exhausted sight is not the remorse expressed by the focus's self.
Watching from the side is a narrative detail unrelated to neglect in relation to God.
Post-judgment disputation illustrates speech that persists after it can no longer repair the outcome.
Turning away from the reminder gives a present counterpart to the focus's neglected response.
A demand for angels is not a distinct link to final regret or mockery.
The condemned openly acknowledge that they were in manifest error.
The root for neglect occurs in divine guardianship, not in the self's culpable omission.
Hidden and disclosed contents of selves are both subject to God's accounting.
The confession of being led astray belongs to the same unrepaired post-judgment reckoning.
It directly presents mockery when a sign is seen.
Joins regret with recurrent mockery of every messenger.
Directly parallels the belated wish for another turn in order to become believers.
Contrasts the call to wonder with the opponents' mocking response.
A bad deed made attractive and the resulting sorrows explain how culpability can remain obscured.
Its surrender at death only indirectly relates to the passage's return-before-death contrast.
Signs within selves have no specific connection to the focus's final self-accusation.
The warning of an unwarned people only broadly concerns missed guidance.
Present submission to God while doing good gives the attainable alternative to the focus's belated wish.
It explicitly depicts disbelievers mocking believers before the Day reverses their apparent status.
God knows what every self earns and the disbelievers will learn the final outcome.
The division between messengerly delivery and divine accounting does not specify the focus's regret.
Personal responsibility is separated from collective rebellion, but no final regret is in view.
What is hidden in the self being made manifest only loosely parallels final disclosure.
Trembling hearts alone do not develop the focus's confession or its cause.
Material boasting does not specifically connect to neglect, regret, or mockery of guidance.
Pharaoh's excess is not tied to the focus's final self-reproach.
Breaking a covenant rebounds upon one's own self, providing a concrete form of self-incurred loss.
Its family obligations and capacity limits do not clarify the focus's final regret.
Its instruction on property stewardship and kind speech is unrelated to the focus's theme.
Mockery of messengers is overtaken by the very warning that was mocked.
Creation from one self and prayer in pregnancy do not illuminate the focus's culpability.
Thankfulness for transport is not a distinct route to regret over neglected duty.
The reminder of creaturely origin modestly counters the self-sufficient arrogance behind rejection.
Resources spent to obstruct God's way become regret before defeat and gathering.
The assembling of souls belongs to the final setting of personal reckoning.
Fear that Pharaoh may exceed bounds is unrelated to the focus's own neglected obligation.
Common human origin and kinship duties do not clarify the focus's final confession.
Thankful use of sacrificial animals does not develop regret, neglect, or mockery.
It concerns a false statement about God, not the focus's failure in relation to God.
A direct cry of regret over a harmful friendship parallels the focus's irreversible self-reproach.
Travel fatigue and a missed meeting point are unrelated to moral neglect.
The challenge about rejecting revelation does not itself portray regret or its final consequence.
No bearer carries another's burden, and purification benefits one's own self before return to God.
The warning that its hearers will remember later anticipates belated recognition.
Professed belief without inward faith is only a loose counterpart to culpable speech.
It explicitly states that misguidance falls upon one's own self and guidance comes by revelation.
Good sent ahead for selves supplies the positive alternative to neglected duty before God's presence.
The warning of sudden earth collapse does not clarify the focus's confession.
It directly attributes wrongdoing to people wronging their own selves, not to God.
The timing of the demanded judgment does not address regret, neglect, or mockery.
Moses' objection to the boat's damage is unrelated to the focus's final moral accounting.
The guardian over every self supports the focus's setting of accountable personal disclosure.
Concealed culpability being brought out offers a limited parallel to eventual exposure.
The disbeliever's final wish to be dust is a direct instance of belated, ineffective speech before judgment.
Its account of belief by God's permission does not clarify the focus's chosen neglect.
Speaking about God without knowledge lightly relates to the focus's reference to God, but not its regret.
Moses acknowledges forgetfulness and asks not to be burdened, unlike the final unrepaired confession.
The wrongdoer's wish that he had taken the messenger's way is a direct final regret over a missed path.
Lot's proposal to his people does not illuminate the focus's themes.
Dismissing a messenger as bewitched is a concrete form of contemptuous rejection.
The distribution of war gains does not clarify final regret or mockery.
The creative command formula is unrelated to the focus's human final speech.
The command to prostrate and worship states the neglected positive response without a specific regret link.
Post-judgment accusations of deceptive influence do not clarify the focus's own neglect.
Rejection of God's signs and severe punishment broadly frame the consequence of denied guidance.
Acknowledging God's ownership without remembering its implication resembles knowledge that fails to reform conduct.
The question to the messengers does not connect to regret, neglect, or mockery.
Each self earns for itself and bears no other burden, directly grounding the focus's personal remorse.
Those who followed false leaders wish for a return so they could disown them, after their deeds become regrets.
Each self confronts its good and evil and wishes its evil were far away.
Repentance remains available for those who turn back before death, defining the opportunity missed in the focus.
It explicitly rejects the deathbed claim of repentance, directly framing remorse that arrives too late.
Those before the Fire wish they could return and no longer deny their Lord's signs.
It exposes the return wish as a response to what was concealed and warns that they would relapse.
The losers ask for intercession or a return so they can act differently after the outcome is realized.
Wrongdoers conceal remorse when they see the punishment, portraying recognition after judgment becomes visible.
Wrongdoers ask for a brief delay to answer the call, after the time for response has passed.
The garden owner wrings his hands in regret over what he spent after its destruction.
Turning from God's reminders and forgetting what one's hands sent ahead directly joins neglect and culpability.
It names the Day of Regret, when the matter is decided while people had been heedless.
Later people neglect prayer and follow desire, then meet the consequence of that neglect.
Turning away from the Quran results in carrying a burden on the Day of Resurrection.
Turning away from divine remembrance gives a concrete present form of the focus's neglected relation to God.
The raised blind person's question continues the consequence of having turned from remembrance.
Forgetting God's signs is answered by being forgotten on the final day.
After punishment falls, the people cry that they were wrongdoers.
The approaching true promise elicits the confession that people had been heedless and wrongdoers.
At death, the wrongdoer asks to be returned in order to perform righteousness.
It denies that requested return and fixes the barrier until resurrection.
The people of the Fire confess that their wretchedness overcame them and that they went astray.
The wrongdoer identifies a companion as having led him away from the remembrance after it came.
The Messenger's complaint that his people abandoned the Quran gives a direct form of neglect of revelation.
When false partners cannot answer, the guilty see the punishment and wish they had been guided.
On the Day excuses neither benefit wrongdoers nor restore an opportunity to make amends.
The guilty lower their heads and ask to be returned so they can act righteously after seeing and hearing.
The final dispute between disbelievers and the weak illustrates post-judgment blame without repair.
The arrogant deny coercion and charge the weak with their own guilt in the final exchange.
Both groups conceal remorse when they see the punishment, while their mutual blame collapses.
The people of the Fire ask to be brought out so they can do righteous work unlike before.
The immediate passage continues with the faces of those who lied about God blackened on the Day of Resurrection.
It contrasts the saved God-conscious with those trapped by the focus's belated regret.
It closes the passage by naming the losers as those who reject God's signs.
Those who disbelieved are reproached for rejecting faith when they were called to it.
The people of the Fire confess their sins after repeated death and life, while seeking a way out.
It states that excuses do not benefit wrongdoers on the Day their excuses are offered.
When wrongdoers see punishment, they ask whether any path exists for a return.
Arriving before God, the person curses the evil companion whose influence had led him astray.
Forgetting the meeting of this Day is answered by being forgotten, with no escape from the Fire.
The hypocrites' final exchange shows a shared appearance of faith exposed too late by their choices.
Before death comes, the person asks for delay so he can give charity and become righteous.
It denies delay once the appointed term arrives, making the prior wish ineffective.
The people of the Blaze admit that listening or reasoning would have kept them from it.
The guilty person wishes to ransom himself from the Day's punishment, but cannot do so.
The question of what brought people into Saqar introduces their confession of neglected obligations.
When Hell is brought near, the person remembers, but that remembrance no longer benefits him.
